answers.note: Strong on safety, JCQ/NEA and positive uses, but it runs well past one page and only gives allowed/not allowed rather than distinct check vs tool levels, with consequences stated as misconduct rather than graduated.
Concise and student-friendly with proportionate consequences, but it has no tiered levels of use and never mentions exam board or coursework rules.
Covers every criterion well, including a clear three-level table, JCQ precedence and a graduated response to misuse, though it is somewhat longer than one page.
Clear, well-timed lesson (58 minutes) with a good catch-it-out task and quiz prompt, but bias appears only as a stretch question.
Very thorough plan covering prediction, fact-checking, bias, learning prompts and safety, but the section 4 sub-timings add up to 20 minutes in an 18-minute slot, so the lesson overruns.
Engaging, timings add up to exactly 60 minutes, with a live bias demo, a four-part learning prompt, school AI levels and a ready-made student sheet.
Excellent: links all three issues to one priority, gives a precise chunk-and-check action step, scripts an 8-minute rehearsal and sets clear success criteria for a dated follow-up.
Warm and practical, but it gives all three issues equal weight with long menus of strategies before prioritising, includes no rehearsal, and defines no success criteria.
One clear priority with a practicable action step, rehearsal and measurable success, though the strengths include invented evidence (greeting students by name) not in the observer's notes.
